title: Punishment that sends shiver down whole England team needed - Vaughan
description: A punishment to “send a shiver down the whole team” may be needed after Brydon Carse became the latest England cricketer involved in a drinking controversy, according to Michael Vaughan.
fullText:
A punishment to "send a shiver down the whole team" may be needed after Brydon Carse became the latest England cricketer involved in a drinking controversy, according to Michael Vaughan.

Pace bowler Carse was briefly placed under arrest on a night out with his Durham team-mates in Derby at the weekend.

The incident is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the England squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's on Thursday.

"Someone is going to have to get a punishment that sends a shiver down the whole England cricket team and right down through the programme, so that everyone knows that if you misbehave or bring any kind of bad reputation on to this team, you know what's going to come," former England captain Vaughan told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It's the only punishment that will really hurt players."

In October, England white-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington, New Zealand, with team-mates Jacob Bethell and Josh Tongue also present.

During the Ashes tour of Australia, opener Ben Duckett was filmed apparently drunk on England's holiday in Noosa.

And in June, former Test captain Ben Stokes and pace bowler Gus Atkinson broke a team curfew and were present when a member of England's security staff was punched by a Saracens rugby player in a London nightclub.

In this latest incident, Carse was with Durham team-mates Stokes and Matthew Potts, all of whom are under England central contracts. In Stokes' case, the England deal remains in place despite his international retirement in June.

It makes a total of eight contracted players who have been involved in or present for late-night incidents in the past year – more than a quarter of the 30 men on England deals.

In this latest occurrence, footage shared on social media on Sunday showed Carse in handcuffs, surrounded by police officers.

Listen to Vaughan, Tufnell and Finn discuss Carse incident on the TMS podcast

And, although Vaughan said it is an "awful look for the England team once again", he would "feel" for Carse if he is made an example of following the other events of the past year.

"I hope Carse is getting good support around him," said Vaughan. "He is a character who can be a little bit loose and if you give him a bit of rope he'll take a huge amount of it. He needs people around him who are giving him better advice.

"I would feel for Carse if he is the one who takes the rap for what has happened over the past nine months, but somewhere, somehow, something has to be done to set a precedent that they won't stand for that behaviour any more."

On Monday, the England and Wales Cricket Board confirmed that the Regulator was investigating and, as a result, 31-year-old Carse had been removed from the squad for the second Test, with his place going to Sonny Baker.

Soon after that, Derbyshire Police said a man in his 30s was arrested on Saturday night, only to be de-arrested a short time later.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," said a police statement.

"However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

This new controversy comes only one game into Joe Root's second spell as Test captain.

Before his first game back in charge, an innings defeat of Pakistan at Headingley, Root called on his players to be "good role models and good human beings".

Now, Root will speak to the media on Tuesday to address the fallout from the Carse incident.

"Joe Root will be absolutely fuming with this," said Vaughan. "He will have been hoping to arrive at Lord's to talk about cricket and his team.

"Now he will have to answer all these questions about discipline, curfews and drinking culture.

"Everything we thought has been brushed under the carpet and moved to one side, we are pretty much back to square one."

Former England spinner Phil Tufnell agreed with Vaughan that a substantial punishment is the only way to ensure players fall in line.

Tufnell, who had multiple brushes with authority during his international career, said: "If you want to stop this, the only way you stop it is say: 'You're not playing for five games.'

"I was made to stand in the corner during my England career, was told: 'You're not available for selection.' It will soon stop. It would be cleared up in a jiffy."

Carse was in the England squad for the first Test but not selected in the final XI. It is unlikely he would have been in the team for the second Test at Lord's, unless one of England's four frontline seamers from Headingley suffered a fitness issue.

Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has more Test wickets than his 58. He was the only member of England's attack to play all five matches in the Ashes series in Australia.

However, he was unavailable at the beginning of the home summer because of an injury, and being removed from the squad for the second Test could push him further down the pecking order.

"Carse is 31 and coming to the autumn of his career," said Tufnell. "You need to keep yourself fit.

"You want to be bowling these long spells for England and making a name for yourself.

"It's probably best not to be doing that [going out so late]. Some of the best in the business have tried and failed at doing that."

title: Watson among Britons through in US Open qualifying
description: Heather Watson is among the British winners in the first round of US Open qualifying as she bids for a first New York main-drawn appearance in five years.
fullText:
Britain's Heather Watson battled back from a set down against Claire Liu to keep alive her hopes of securing a first US Open main-draw appearance in five years.

The 34-year-old Watson beat sixth seed Liu 4-6 6-2 6-4 in the first round of qualifying in New York.

Watson almost let a double-break lead slip in the final set but held firm to set up a meeting with Spain's Angela Fita Boluda.

Toby Samuel, Jacob Fearnley, Billy Harris and Harry Wendelken all progressed in men's qualifying.

Samuel, seeking to reach the US Open main draw for the first time, fought back against Italy's Francesco Maestrelli to win 6-7 (2-7) 6-3 6-1 and set up a meeting with fellow Briton Harris.

Harris progressed with a 6-1 6-3 win against Peru's Gonzalo Bueno.

Fearnley claimed a 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 victory over Spain's Roberto Carballes Baena to set up a meeting with Frenchman Luka Pavlovic.

Wendelken will meet Swiss player Remy Bertola after overcoming Italy's Stefano Travaglia 6-4 3-6 6-3.

However, Liam Broady lost 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 against Italy's Marco Cecchinato, while Felix Gill was beaten by Italian Francesco Passaro 7-6 (7-3) 6-2.

Players must come through three rounds of qualifying to reach the singles main draw, which gets under way on Sunday.

Williams and Alcaraz to play US Open mixed doubles

Injured Sinner & Draper withdraw from US Open

China's two-time US Open quarter-finalist Zheng Qinwen, contesting a Grand Slam qualifying event for the first time since the 2022 Australian Open, defeated compatriot Xiaodi You 6-3 6-2.

The 23-year-old, who has fallen to 121st in the world since undergoing elbow surgery last year, will meet France's Clara Burel next.

Meanwhile, Brazilian world number 26 Joao Fonseca has announced he will miss the tournament because of an abdominal injury.

The 20-year-old French Open quarter-finalist said he would require "more time to fully recover so I can compete at a high level".

In the mixed doubles competition, Britons Henry Patten and Lloyd Glasspool will both seek to beat some of the sport's biggest stars after coming through two qualifying matches on Monday.

The US Open mixed doubles was controversially revamped last year to include singles stars in a bid to attract more attention to the format.

Under the new format, the top six pairs with the best combined singles rankings received direct entry into the main draw, with another eight receiving wildcards.

The tournament now takes place over three days in the week before the main draw began, and features a shorter scoring system with only four games required to win a set in matches before the final, no 'advantage' scoring and 10-point match tie-breaks instead of a third set throughout.

Both Patten and Glasspool had to come through qualifying with their respective partners on Monday.

Patten, a two-time winner of the men's doubles competition at Wimbledon, and Czech team-mate Katerina Siniakova defeated Americans Peyton Stearns and Christian Harrison in straight sets in their second qualifying match.

Next, Patten and Siniakova - the respective men's and women's world number ones in doubles - will take on 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic and top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka in the first round of the main draw.

After defeating El Salvador's Marcelo Arevalo and France's Kristina Mladenovic, Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe will face 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams and seven-time major winner Carlos Alcaraz.

Alcaraz will be playing his first match in four months after recovering from a wrist injury, while Williams is making her return to the sport after a four-year absence.

title: Why one of Trump’s favorite economic statistics is nearly meaningless
description: President Donald Trump says not to believe the many polls finding that most Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy. On Friday, to argue that his numbers should be much better, he cited a nearly meaningless fact he portrayed as a major accomplishment.
fullText:
President Donald Trump says not to believe the many polls finding that most Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy. On Friday, to argue that his numbers should be much better, he cited a nearly meaningless fact he portrayed as a major accomplishment.

"I'll see a poll," he said at a rally in South Carolina, "and it'll say, 'Trump is at 44% on the economy.' How can it be at 44? We have more people working now than ever before."

Trump heralded the same fact later in the speech: "Remember when I say, and I'll say it again and again: There are more people working today in the United States of America than at any time in the history of our country." And then, emphasizing the supposed importance of the fact, he repeated it a third time.

It's not clear whether Trump is genuinely unaware this fact is insignificant or whether he is knowingly hyping an insignificant fact for political gain. Regardless, touting the fact "again and again" is unlikely to do anything for his economic approval — because the fact tells us almost nothing about the state of the economy.

The number of people working in the US generally rises over time simply because the population rises over time. With the exception of recessions, like those caused by the financial crisis of 2008 or the Covid-19 crisis of 2020, the number of employed people tends to just get higher as the years pass.

"There are more Americans working because there are more Americans. That's the entire analysis," Justin Wolfers, a University of Michigan professor of public policy and economics, wrote in his newsletter earlier this month.

Every US president since at least 1948, when modern federal data collection began, could have accurately said at some point during their tenure that more people were working in the US than ever before. That clearly isn't because each of these presidents was presiding over a pristine economy.

The cost of living, not the state of the labor market, has almost certainly been the key driver of Trump's dismal economic polling this year. But even if you're looking only at jobs, there are much better ways to gauge the situation than the statistic Trump keeps citing. These other metrics show his second-term economy is far from historically strong.

You can look, for example, at the employment-population ratio, which measures the percentage of the population ages 16 and over that is employed. It's down from 60.1% in January 2025, the month of Trump's second inauguration, to 58.9% in July 2026 — lower than it was during the entirety of Joe Biden's last three years as president.

title: Victims describe 'house of terror' abuse by mother, grandmother and stepfather
description: Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented.
fullText:
A mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail.

Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012.

Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuse

Freeman was sentenced to 18 months probation, 240 hours of unpaid work, and a 12-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody.

Stephen was ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and given 18 months probation.

And McColl was sentenced to 220 hours of unpaid work, 18 months probation, and an 11-month restriction of liberty order.

Victims William and Meaghann Murphy, who are now 25 and 28, told BBC Scotland News the violence and cruelty they experienced as children became normal.

William said he was "utterly disappointed" at what he described as the "leniency" of the sentence.

"Violence and psychological terror resulted in nothing more than unpaid work and a curfew," he said.

"This system has failed my sisters and me, but we refuse to let it silence us. We must do better. We must stop child abusers from walking away with a slap on the wrist."

Their younger sister, Rebekah Simpson, 23, said the abuse she received had had a lifelong impact on her mental and physical health.

She said she felt that the court did not fully consider the impact the experience had had on her - but she was not disappointed with the sentences.

"Not having to speak to them again is justice for me," she said.

"I want to be able to walk the streets and know they will be punished if they try and approach me."

The abuse happened at an address in Balloch, Dunbartonshire, and at a flat in Aberdeen's Bedford Avenue.

A trial heard that Freeman, now of Cullen, Moray, had created a "house of terror" for the children.

"The things that stick out for me were the anger, the violent outbursts that would come from my mother," Meaghann said.

"William and I were both locked in a room and because I was bursting for the toilet I had to take all my clothes out of my bottom drawer and use that.

"She went ballistic about it. I got slapped about for that. After that, instead of letting us out the room, she just put a bucket in the room.

"So my experience from the get-go has been just straight-up cruelty."

She described being deprived of food for days at a time and said locks were placed on cupboards to prevent the children helping themselves.

The court heard Freeman repeatedly struck the children with a metal-studded belt.

William said: "For as long as I can remember, family life was chaotic and unpredictable, and at times quite hostile. We were often made to sleep on the floor as a punishment.

"Sometimes when we had been really bad, they called it sleep deprivation, where they got us to stand up, like in a line, and we were made to stay awake.

"Your mind starts to play tricks on you. I remember starting to see faces in the wall.

"If we were dozing off or showed any sign that we weren't taking it seriously, things were thrown at us, or we were shouted at, and the punishment was then extended."

He said his older sister tried to protect him.

"Meaghann was effectively like a human mattress," he recalled.

"She took the brunt of sleeping on the concrete, and she would then let myself cuddle into her and rub the back of my head.

"She tried to shield us from as much as possible. She was our protector."

Meaghann said she continued to struggle with feelings of guilt over what happened, as she could not offer more protection.

"I'll live with it for the rest of my life," she said.

"I will never forgive myself for the things I had to see and I couldn't do anything about it.

"I know I was a child, but I didn't see it like that at the time and I still struggle to see it that way."

Rebekah said she has had lifelong mental health problems, has been diagnosed with personality disorder, and has had substance misuse issues.

She described her childhood as "very conflicted".

"There was moments that were happy," she said.

"There's a lot of fond memories amongst all the bad, but the bad outweighs the good.

"There was a lot of laughs, but more often than not there were a lot of tears and a lot of reasons to feel alone."

Police Scotland launched an investigation in 2022 after William made a statement.

The siblings said they decided to speak out in the hope their story may help others.

"I feel like this is the first time we've ever really been given a platform that we can use to make a difference in some way," Meaghann said.

"Even if one person was to take something positive from it, then I've done my bit."

William said he hoped sharing their experiences would help others recognise the signs of abuse.

He concluded: "My mother, grandmother and stepfather are evil, barbaric and cruel.

"But it hasn't changed us. Not in the way they wanted it to anyway."

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Solicitor Andrew Ormiston, for Freeman, said she maintained her innocence, and had expressed "confusion" over why the complainers had made the allegations.

John McLeod, for Stephen, said she also continued to maintain her innocence.

Debbie Ginniver, for McColl, said he had admitted the offences, did not seek to justify or excuse his behaviour, and had shown "deep remorse".

Sheriff Findlater told Freeman that "shame has been brought to your name".

He told the three first offenders there were alternative sentences to custody.

Alison McKenzie, procurator fiscal for Grampian, Highlands and Islands, said the trio were adults when they "knowingly and deliberately subjected these children to a horrific catalogue of mistreatment".

She said: "The evidence showed that, rather than providing the care, affection and security every child deserves, they engaged in a sustained pattern of cruelty, degradation and harmful behaviour.

"We hope this prosecution reassures others who have experienced child abuse that they will be listened to, treated with dignity and supported throughout the criminal justice process, regardless of when the offending took place."

Det Insp Kerry McCombie, of Police Scotland, added: "The abuse spanned across the childhood years of the victims and I'd like to pay tribute to them for their bravery to bring this case before the courts."

If you or someone you know have been affected by child abuse, you can find more details of help and support at the BBC Action Line.

title: Vulnerable GOP senator breaks with Trump on 2 key issues as Vance makes stop without her
description: Susan Collins skips JD Vance's Maine visit while opposing Trump's 50% tariffs on Canada and new postal service rules restricting mail-in voting.
fullText:
Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a moderate Republican seeking re-election in a blue-leaning state, is not joining Vice President JD Vance on Monday as he stops in her home state of Maine.

Collins, who at times has opposed President Donald Trump's legislative priorities, is a top target for Democrats this year as she runs in a midterm race that's among roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP holds onto its slim Senate majority.

Vance's stop in Maine comes as Collins opposes Trump's move this past weekend to impose 50% tariffs on a range of goods from Canada, which shares a long border with Maine. And the senator is also opposed to new U.S. Postal Service rules that, if implemented, could rein in mail-in voting.

The vice president on Monday delivered remarks in Brewer, Maine, at Compotech, a defense technology manufacturer. It's the second stop this year by Vance in Maine and the second time that Collins has not teamed up with the vice president.

Susan Collins Drops Brutal Reminder Of Democrat Challenger Rocked By Accusations

"I am already scheduled on Monday, so I will not be able to join the vice president," Collins told reporters on Saturday.

The Senate was in session when Vance held an event in Bangor, Maine, in May, and Collins stayed in Washington. The senator holds a historic attendance record of casting over 10,000 consecutive roll call votes in the Senate dating back three decades.

But Collins, speaking to reporters as she marched in the annual Madison-Anson Days parade, her seventh parade this summer, highlighted that she teamed up last week with Energy Secretary Chris Wright when he stopped in Maine to tour a federally funded battery storage project in Lincoln built on the site of a closed paper mill.

"I really appreciated Secretary Wright's presence," Collins said.

What The Latest Fox News Poll In Maine's Crucial Senate Race Shows

Collins, who was one of a small group of Republicans who voted to convict Trump in a 2021 Senate trial after the House impeached him following the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, has at times voted against the Trump administration's wishes.

"I still think imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake," Collins said on Saturday.

Collins also referred to the proposed U.S. Post Office rule to implement a Trump executive order to rein in mail-in voting by refusing to deliver absentee ballots in states that have not turned over their raw voter rolls to the Justice Department or Department of Homeland Security.

"Mail-in ballots are very important to the people of Maine," Collins said. "I do not support restrictions that make it more difficult for seniors to cast votes on Election Day via the mail."

Collins says she supports the House version of the federal SAVE America Act (Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act), which mandates documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote and a photo ID for federal elections. But she joined three other Republicans and all Democrats to vote against advancing a Senate version of the bill, which is a top Trump priority.

Collins has also taken issue with the Trump administration over its crackdown on illegal immigration, and its aggressive deportation efforts. The administration received backlash following the fatal shootings by federal enforcement agents of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota who were protesting immigration operations. And the issue flared again this summer, after a fatal ICE shooting in Biddeford, Maine.

Democrats, including her Senate challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have repeatedly linked her to Trump, and heavily criticized her for her past funding for ICE.

Democracy '26: Stay Up To Date With The Fox News Election Hub

Collins is the only Republican senator running for re-election in a state then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 election. And highlighting her differences with the president and his administration may be beneficial to Collins as she woos independent voters and even some Democrats.

Vance, during his May stop in Maine, said, "Sometimes I get frustrated with Susan Collins."

"I almost wish that she was more partisan. But the thing I love about Susan is she is independent, because Maine is an independent state. And, frankly, if she was as partisan as I sometimes wish that she was, she would not be a good fit for the people of Maine," Vance continued.

Vance added, "Let's give a shoutout to Susan Collins, who's doing a great job."

Jackson's campaign, in a social media post ahead of Vance's visit, called the vice president "Susan's pal."

The vice president reiterated those sentiments in his Monday address in Brewer, Maine, calling Collins his "dear friend."

"As you know, Susan is the most independent member of the United States Senate and, as the president of the United States Senate, she sometimes makes my job a little bit harder. But she makes it harder because she's coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party… she comes to work every single day and fights for the great people of Maine and I've seen it," Vance said.

Jackson, in a social media post and video ahead of Vance's visit, took aim at Vance and Collins.

"I'm sure JD Vance loves her because she's doing everything that he wants for her, but she's not doing it for Maine people," Jackson argued in an accompanying video.

Vance was joined in Brewer by former two-term Republican Gov. Paul LePage, who is the GOP nominee in Maine's 2nd Congressional District.

The most rural district, the largest in the eastern U.S., is a top flip opportunity for the GOP, with moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Golden declining to seek re-election this year.

title: Clarence Thomas scorches racial litmus tests policing thought: ‘Stay Black and die’
description: Clarence Thomas compared restrictions on Black conservatives' viewpoints to racial segregation in a wide-ranging interview with Sen. Ted Cruz.
fullText:
Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas rejected the idea that Black Americans should be expected to hold particular political views because of their race during a rare interview with Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz.

"We had this saying [that there are] only two things I have to do: stay Black and die," Thomas told Cruz, responding to a comment about the conservative justice having an individualist streak. "That was a retort to people who had these sort of requirements for us, these these mandates for us because of our skin color … But at any rate, they think that here's the way you're supposed to think. Again, here's your skin color. There's this kind of deterministic view that you're supposed to think this because we say so."

"And I, of course, declined that invitation. And so now that means that something, that I'm a walking contradiction because I've deviated from their perception of what I should think," the justice added while speaking on the "Verdict with Ted Cruz" podcast.

Democrat Lawmaker Calls Clarence Thomas An 'Uncle Tom' And 'Lynchman' After Supreme Court Redistricting Ruling

Thomas, who is Black, grew up poor in segregated Georgia, initially living in his parents' wooden shack in Pin Point and later in Savannah with his grandparents. As a child, Thomas was raised speaking Gullah, a creole language derived from English spoken by the descendants of African slaves.

At the College of the Holy Cross, he initially embraced left-wing Black nationalism, admired Malcolm X and helped establish the school's Black Student Union. Thomas began moving right after participating in a violent 1970 protest in Cambridge, Massachusetts, later saying his shame over the episode prompted him to reject left-wing activism and reconsider the self-reliance preached by his grandfather.

Clarence Thomas Warns America: Liberty Dies When We Choose Comfort Over Courage

To further explain his point, Thomas compared efforts to dictate which ideas Black Americans should embrace to the restrictions of racial segregation.

"Here's what I've asked people. I said, 'When I was a kid, the Savannah Public Library was segregated.' I said, 'Do you think it was right that the Savannah Public Library was segregated?' Oh, no. You should have been able to go in," Thomas stated. "I said, 'What if they allowed me in but said I couldn't go to certain floors? That would be wrong.' I said, "What about if they said you couldn't go to certain stacks?' Well, that would be wrong. 'What if they had certain books marked that were off limits to me?' That would be wrong."

Black Gop Congressman Shuts Down Race Question Following Supreme Court Redistricting Ruling

"Then my question is, why is it then that you have a problem with me embracing certain ideas in certain books? What's the difference?' Thomas went on.

title: US set for largest mass visa revocation in history targeting up to 200,000 foreigners, officials say
description: The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States.  If it happ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum status in the United States. If it happens, the move would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges.

Unless challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The action will be taken in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," said State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott.

He declined to comment on the number of visas that might be revoked, saying "as the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

The revocations would not necessarily result in their immediate deportation, the officials said. Most of those with asylum cases currently pending would be recategorized but would lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the revocations are not final yet.

Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term last year, his administration has steadily ramped up restrictions on visa applicants — demanding more information about their social media histories, requiring the posting of expensive bonds for the processing of visas, and outright banning the issuance of visas to citizens of certain countries.

In a social media post on Monday, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau called out people who he said try to use tourist and business visas to get into the United States and then apply for asylum.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law." Landau cited the case of a Colombian citizen who came to the U.S. in 2015 on a tourist visa and then applied for asylum.

B1 visas are generally issued for business trips and B2 visas are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care. It was not immediately clear from the documents or the officials how many of these visa holders are seeking or have sought asylum in the United States and would be affected by the revocations.

Current applicants for B1 and B2 visas are asked to affirm that they will not apply for asylum in the United States and prove that they intend to return to their home countries.

In the past 18 months, the State Department has revoked about 175,000 visas for people who have been convicted or accused of crimes ranging from drunken driving to rape and robbery, as well as for people who have spoken out publicly against U.S. policies, particularly in the Middle East.

The administration has also moved to crack down on so-called birth tourism, a practice the administration claims is used by foreign pregnant women to come to the United States to give birth so that their child will benefit from birthright citizenship. Trump has tried several times to end birthright citizenship, but those challenges have been rejected by courts, including the Supreme Court.

The State Department documents obtained by the AP suggest screening of current B1 and B2 visa holders began after the State Department received information about asylum requests from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: Deportees who refused to exit a US flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
description: Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another ‌African nation that signed a third-country de...
fullText:
DAKAR, Senegal (AP) — Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another ‌African nation that signed a third-country deportation agreement with the Trump administration, a person on the plane and a lawyer in contact with the six said Monday.

Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren't their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled.

The group who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday include four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and lawyer said.

A Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was "not their country" and that they would face danger there. They were then separated from the others, he said. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals.

He said the other passengers got off in Liberia because they feared officers would force them.

Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said the deportees who resisted leaving the plane in Liberia were told they would be returned to the United States but instead were flown to Malabo city in Equatorial Guinea.

"It was a really heartbreaking and chaotic scene when they arrived in Malabo on Thursday," Yoon said.

Some arrived in chains and in extreme distress, she said, including the Cameroonian woman and one of the Cuban men, who Yoon said has a large abdominal growth and uses a colostomy bag that must be drained regularly.

There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added.

Conditions at the hotel have worsened in recent months, Yoon said, with food sometimes withheld and guards accused of threatening, beating and choking some of the migrants.

Equatorial Guinea's government did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.

Under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration, Equatorial Guinea's all-powerful president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, has turned the hotel owned by his family into a prison for asylum seekers deported from the U.S.

title: Supreme Court sides with Trump administration on mail voting restrictions ahead of midterms
description: The Supreme Court opened a path Monday for possible implementation of President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much can be put in place before...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court opened a path Monday for possible implementation of President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, though it remains unclear how much can be put in place before the fast-approaching midterm elections.

The decision leaves room for additional court challenges that could further slow Trump's order, and other similar cases have already been filed. The U.S. Postal Service laid out how it would implement the order last week, but time is running short to impose major changes. North Carolina is sending out ballots Sept. 4 overseas and to military voters, and other states will quickly follow suit in just a few weeks.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority didn't decide the legality of Trump's order, instead ruling that states who sued did not have the legal right to challenge it.

While the emergency order is not final, it does have the potential to create chaos around voting across the country, with Trump often questioning the integrity of elections and the nation's highest court again the possible arbiter of a political controversy.

"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell," the majority wrote in an unsigned order.

The three liberal-leaning justices publicly dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson writing that the rule "lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges."

New York Attorney General Letitia James foreshadowed more legal fights ahead, calling the decision a "painful setback" but vowing it would "not be the final word."

The court's order opens a path for the administration to begin action to restrict mail voting, but it also could lead to further litigation that could freeze the federal government again.

"This is just the first inning of a very fast nine-inning game," said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame University.

Mail balloting has long been a favorite target for Trump, who has claimed that it breeds fraud despite strong evidence to the contrary and his own use of the voting method.

Trump's executive order, signed in March, calls on his administration to create lists of eligible voters and orders the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists. New requirements released Friday would forbid the Postal Service from sending mail ballots from any state that does not comply with Trump's order.

A Postal Service spokesperson did not immediately respond messages seeking comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia sued to block the order. They argued that the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to run elections, and Trump's changes could lead to chaos and partisan abuse.

"The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall's elections would be extreme," attorneys for the states wrote. Dozens of state and local election officials weighed in, asking the justices to leave the order frozen while election preparations are already underway.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Monday the order was aimed at making it "harder for Americans to vote" in the pivotal elections for control of Congress, and vowed that Democrats would "fight every attempt to hijack mail-in voting and rig the rules before voters have their say this November."

A judge in Massachusetts blocked the plan for the midterm elections in those states. An appeals court upheld her decision. She later granted a second order blocking it nationwide in a separate case, another remaining stumbling block for Trump administration.

The Justice Department appealed to the Supreme Court on procedural grounds in late July, arguing that the states sued too soon. They also pointed to another ruling out of Washington, where a judge allowed Trump's order to proceed. An appeals court backed that decision, while still leaving room for future court action if the changes are implemented.

Federal attorneys argued that the Massachusetts order "blocks the government's ability to finalize and implement the President's proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November."

A dozen Republican-leaning states supported the federal government in their own appeal before the high court, saying states would have input on the final voter lists.

The Supreme Court has previously ruled against Trump-backed arguments on mail-in ballots, finding in a 5-4 decision that states can count ballots that arrive after Election Day. That case was decided after full briefing and arguments, rather than on the court's emergency docket.

Trump has blamed mail voting — without credible evidence — for his loss to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. He has promoted the proposed changes in his executive order as safeguards to keep non-U.S. citizens from voting.

He's also repeatedly pressed for the passage of the legislation that requires proof of citizenship to vote. Noncitizen voting has been shown to be exceedingly rare, and is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.

Using mail ballots has become increasingly popular with voters of both parties, with about 30% of all ballots cast that way during the 2024 presidential election, according to federal data. The process also is secure. A 2025 Brookings Institution study found only about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.

David Becker, a former justice department lawyer who co-wrote a book debunking Trump's 2020 election lies, said the high court created "pure chaos leading up to the midterm elections, waiting weeks after an administration filing, and just days before mail ballots go out, to completely rewrite the rules."

title: El-Sayed distances himself from Hasan Piker after disturbing remarks about Jewish Americans
description: Abdul El-Sayed distances himself from Hasan Piker after the Twitch streamer's comments about Jewish Americans sparked a bipartisan backlash.
fullText:
Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed is trying to put some distance between himself and one of his top supporters, Hasan Piker, after the controversial streamer sparked a new firestorm.

El-Sayed, who is facing off against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in battleground Michigan in a high-stakes Senate showdown, on Monday emphasized in a statement, "I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople."

The statement from El-Sayed came after Piker, on his stream last week, featured an image of state Sen. Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss, who is Jewish, has said that people are sharing a fake audio clip of him claiming that his entire reason for running for Congress is to make sure that America continues to support Israel.

"If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker warned.

Democrats 'Who Never Voted Republican' Backing This Gop Senate Nominee

Piker, who endorsed El-Sayed for the Democratic nomination and appeared at some of the candidate's campaign events including a primary night party in Detroit, has repeatedly stood by his numerous past comments critical of Israel over its ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza.

Piker's latest comments have been blasted by a growing number of Republicans and Democrats since they grabbed attention this past weekend. Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten of Michigan charged that Piker is "a hack who thrives on hate."

Rogers, in a social media post on Sunday, took aim at both Piker and El-Sayed.

"More calls for violence coming out of the El-Sayed campaign," Rogers said. And he claimed, "Here is his running mate, Hasan Piker, saying that if AMERICAN JEWS support Israel, they will be violently targeted because of it."

Rogers added, "Absolutely DISGUSTING. If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all. We're waiting, Abdul…"

Democracy '26: Stay Up To Date With The Fox News Election Hub

El-Sayed, in his statement, wrote, "I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past."

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters. Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk," he added.

In an apparent jab at Rogers and other Republicans who have repeatedly tied El-Sayed to Piker, the Democratic nominee wrote that "while politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we're going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare. Because that's what Michiganders keep asking about.'

Responding, Rogers on Monday afternoon argued, "Abdul's attempt at distancing himself from this violent and hateful rhetoric now that he and Hasan won the primary is the epitome of what a conman does — says one thing when it serves him and another when it doesn't. His rhetoric is causing fear in Michigan communities, is un-American, and makes him unfit to represent our state."

A former Wayne County Health Department director, El-Sayed, if elected in November, would make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. The epidemiologist who unsuccessfully ran for governor as an insurgent candidate in 2018 has made support for Medicare for all a major component of his campaign and has also called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Check Out The Latest Fox News Poll In Michigan's Blockbuster Senate Race

But it's El-Sayed's stance and comments on Israel that have offended some Jewish people in Michigan, a state that also has a large Arab and Muslim population.

El-Sayed used the word "bloodthirsty" to characterize Israel's military moves in Gaza in an MS NOW interview this month and accused Israeli leadership of genocide against Palestinians. He has argued against unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel, as have other progressive politicians. And El-Sayed has repeatedly declined to directly answer whether Israel has the right to exist.

But El-Sayed has also repeatedly stated that he stands "in solidarity with my Jewish sisters and brothers" to "condemn antisemitism."

After falling just 20,000 votes shy of winning the U.S. Senate election in Michigan two years ago, Rogers is urging Democrats, including Jewish voters, to cross party lines and vote for him as he makes a second straight Senate bid.

What The Latest Fox News Power Rankings In The Midterm Races Show

After a combustible and divisive Democratic Senate primary in which El-Sayed narrowly edged more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens for the nomination, Rogers is heavily courting Democrats disaffected with their left-wing nominee.

A key part of Rogers' pitch is directed toward Jewish Democrats, who are uneasy with El–Sayed's vocal criticism of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza and who are outraged by El-Sayed's association with Piker.

"I usually vote Democrat, but I'm going to be voting for Mike Rogers," Rabbi Asher Lopatin said as he stood next to Rogers late last week as the former congressman and former FBI agent unveiled his Democrats for Mike coalition at a campaign event on Detroit's west side.

Lopatin, a rabbi in suburban Detroit who has made trips to the Middle East in search of peace between Israel and its Arab neighbors, argued that El-Sayed "has shown contempt for the Jewish community and, frankly, for American values by making Hasan Piker, a vicious antisemite and racist, his campaign surrogate and somebody he buddies up with."

Meanwhile, some Jewish leaders in Michigan are circulating an open letter urging Jewish Democrats and independents in the Great Lakes battleground state to sign their names in support of Rogers. The news was first reported this week by the Jewish Insider and confirmed by Fox News Digital.

"This is sort of a do-or-die moment," a person involved with the letter who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely told Fox News Digital. "There are many lifelong Democrats who are feeling homeless. ... It's not just a leftward drift but has turned into an anti-Jewish drift as well."

But Joan Lowenstein, endorsement chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, doesn't condone the letter and told Fox News Digital her group is keeping its distance.

"We are a part of the Michigan Democratic Party, and are not going to advocate that anyone vote for a Republican," she said.

But Lowenstein, who also sits on the Michigan Democratic Party Central Committee, said those behind the letter "are passionate about this and feel it's an existential issue, and I think that represents a lot of people. And, so, they have to do what they have to do."

El-Sayed Communications Director Roxie Richner last week told Fox News Digital, "Abdul has always stressed the importance of differentiating between criticizing the state of Israel and antisemitism."

She said El-Sayed "remains in regular dialogue with Jewish leaders across the state while building the broadest possible coalition to defeat Rogers, restore Democratic control of the U.S. Senate and throw sand in the gears of Trump's agenda."

Canadians spoke out across social media. Some told Business Insider they were committed to not buying American products.

Canadians have long been boycotting American goods. Then came the latest wave of tariffs.

Trade talks between the US and Canada fell apart on Friday, and the US enforced a 50% tariff on some Canadian goods the following day. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney quickly proposed dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs.

Many Canadians were already fed up with their neighbors down south. Some previously chose to stop buying American products; others suspended their travel to America.

Aug 24 (Reuters) - Gold rose to its highest in more than three months on Monday, building on gains from last ‌week as a muted dollar boosted appeal, while investors awaited U.S. ‌inflation data and remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh this week for signals on the ​interest-rate path.

Spot gold was up 0.7% at $4,635.25 per ounce by 0838 GMT, hitting its highest level since May 15, while U.S. gold futures rose 0.2% to $4,691.10.

Bullion rose more than 5% last week after the U.S. Treasury Department's buyback support plan ‌pushed the dollar lower, making ⁠greenback-priced bullion more affordable for foreign investors.

"The consolidation of gold prices above $4,600, and the potential for further gains, will depend ⁠to a large extent on the U.S. dollar remaining under pressure and Treasury yields stabilizing at current levels or declining further," ActivTrades senior analyst Ricardo Evangelista said.

Market ​participants are now awaiting the July ‌Personal Consumption Expenditure price index due on Wednesday and Warsh's speech at the Jackson Hole Symposium on Friday to gauge the policymakers' outlook on interest rates.

Traders are pricing in about a 36% chance of a rate-hike in September, with a 64% chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged, according to the ‌CME FedWatch Tool.

title: Human remains found in Tucson’s vast desert have fueled speculation about a link to Nancy Guthrie. Here’s what’s going on
description: Officials say there’s no known connection Nancy Guthrie, but the discovery highlights the high number of people who are found dead in the desert every year.
fullText:
As the chief medical examiner for a county that stores the most human remains in the nation, Greg Hess has for decades been accustomed to the many that arrive at his office every year after being found in the vast and rugged southern Arizona desert.

People traveling through the remote Sonoran Desert die from its extreme heat, harsh conditions and rough terrain. Most of the people who are found dead there every year are assumed to be migrants, Hess says, because of the desert's location on the southern border.

But ever since Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her home in Tucson nearly seven months ago, the first question Hess says he asks himself when a set of human remains arrives at his office in Pima County for examination is whether they could be hers.

"Every time somebody found a body in the wash or somewhere else in southern Arizona over the past few months, there's speculation that it's the person everybody's interested in," Hess told CNN.

Questions swirled last week when human remains were found in the desert about 15 miles from where the mother of NBC "Today" show host Savannah Guthrie lived.

While announcing the discovery, authorities said there was "no indication" the remains belonged to Guthrie but stopped short of fully ruling out a connection. The sheriff's office later declined to say why that determination was made, when the remains were found or who found them when asked by CNN.

Pima County has for years ranked among the highest in the nation for the number of unidentified human remains, according to the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System (NamUs).

The fact a majority of them belong to people who traveled from another country and the conditions of the desert itself both complicate efforts to identify remains, therefore hindering missing persons cases, experts say.

Heat, sunlight exposure, monsoons, animals and others speed up decomposition, Hess says. Many of the human remains that arrive at his office are either fully or partially skeletonized, he added.

The national spotlight on the area since Guthrie's disappearance has in turn led to a greater public awareness about the many people who go missing or die in the sprawling desert and reveals just how many families are also searching for answers.

Last Monday, sheriff's deputies were seen at the reported location of the human remains, on a hillside covered in saguaro cacti overlooking a busy four-lane highway in southwest Tucson.

The residential area, which sits on the outskirts of the city limit, is one turn off a road called Ajo Way that leads to a handful of homes with long driveways.

Just three months earlier, another discovery of human remains near Guthrie's home also made headlines. Meanwhile, investigators continue to run lab analyses on DNA found at her home as the desperate search for Guthrie continues.

Many of the human remains found in the Sonoran Desert, which covers over 100,000 miles, are believed to be people who have often died from dehydration or exposure to other harsh conditions, according to experts including Hess.

The desert's location on the southern border has led to many migrants attempting to cross it by using dangerous backcountry routes, the experts said.

All four of the land border states — California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas — have significantly high rates of human remains discovered and unidentified persons cases every year, according to Dr. Molly Kaplan, post-doctoral scholar at Texas State University who also works for its program focused on border crossing-related deaths in Texas.

Anthropology experts like Kaplan consider deaths in those regions an ongoing "chronic mass disaster," she says.

Most of the roughly 150 sets of human remains that Hess says are discovered in Pima County every year turn up after monsoon season ends in late September, said Bradley Bartos, assistant professor at the University of Arizona.

Monsoons bring extreme winds and flash flooding that can free the remains from wedged or remote positions and push them "down-wash into a more eminently discoverable place," Bartos said.

"Those same reasons explain why there is very low probability those recently discovered remains will turn out to be related to the Nancy Guthrie case," Bartos said.

Hess says he's always been able to quickly rule out that any of the human remains found in Pima County were consistent with Guthrie.

He says his office receives up to 5,000 death reports yearly and stores about 600 sets of human remains, which is the most of any county nationwide.

In comparison, Tucson's county seat is storing 300 more unidentified human remains than Los Angeles County — an area home to 9 million more residents, according to NamUs.

Pima County, however, is set up to handle the workload. "We've had a lot of experience with people dying in desert areas," Hess says.

It's unusual for even one anthropologist to be on staff at a medical examiner's office, but there are three at Hess' office, which he says is because, "We just get the volume of skeletal remains."

The discovery of human remains that set off a firestorm of questions about a possible link to Guthrie developed during an agonizing, monthslong search for the beloved mother.

The investigation continues to produce few public leads despite intensive efforts to find her.

But the lack of clarity from officials doesn't mean they've hit a dead end; There may be "practical law enforcement concerns behind their silence," according to CNN Chief Law Enforcement and Intelligence Analyst John Miller.

Authorities saying there is no indication the remains are tied to the Guthrie case and a statement officially ruling it out are "two different things," Miller said.

"The first requires an investigative judgment based on what they see, but the second requires actual scientific evidence," he said. "Authorities understand that ruling out a connection before they are certain would only draw more criticism to a case where they have already heard their share."

But the scientific evidence needed to rule out that connection could be complicated if the remains are damaged, said Miller.

With a complete set of remains, a forensic pathologist could determine fairly quickly whether the bones belonged to a male or female, but without, that task could prove more difficult, he added.

The condition of the remains is unclear and officials did not respond to CNN's request for comment, but Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos said the remains had already been at the location "for an extended period of time" by the time they were discovered.

In the desert, it's common for human remains to be damaged and become skeletal much faster than in other environments — even as soon as a month or two, according to Hess.

Anthropologists such as those at Hess' office work with the bones to create biological profiles that will help determine the sex and estimate the age, according to Kaplan. At that point, they need to rely on DNA to complete the process, which can be difficult to extract when the remains are fragile, she said.

Once they are recovered, the remains are often sun-bleached, scavenged and without any recognizable features, Kaplan said. Remains in the desert might not only get damaged but also scattered over large areas, she added.

Damage to the remains creates challenges for families who don't know where to report their loved one missing, as well as for law enforcement trying to coordinate search efforts and recover remains, she added.

Even with the volume of lives lost in deserts, experts believe "the numbers of recorded remains found in these environments is a gross underestimate," Kaplan said.

Taking into consideration all of the people who haven't been discovered, it would be impossible to quantify the number of lives lost in the area every year and the lasting impact on those left searching for them.

To help families with missing loved ones get closure, the Pima County medical examiner started a program in 2018, making it the only county nationwide to store skeletal remains in an air-conditioned space, according to the National Association of Counties.

Medical examiners typically cremate remains after a certain period of time if they are not claimed, which prevents family members from making an identification at a later time, Hess said.

Even though it comes as a byproduct of the devastating and ongoing search for Nancy Guthrie since her apparent kidnapping in February, Kaplan says any awareness of what anthropologists call the "chronic mass disaster" – or the countless yearly deaths near the southern border – is important.

"It makes sense that people would have questions when there's a specific person who is being looked for," Kaplan said. "But the reality is that this is happening quite regularly and actually needs to be talked about more."

"Every missing person counts," she added.

CNN's Julianna Bragg contributed to this report.

title: US Postal Service issues new rule for mail ballots, but its impact on the midterms is uncertain
description: The U.S. Postal Service unveiled new requirements for mail ballots less than two weeks before some states begin sending them and in time for the conservative majority of the Supreme Court to clear the...
fullText:
The U.S. Postal Service unveiled new requirements for mail ballots less than two weeks before some states begin sending them and in time for the conservative majority of the Supreme Court to clear the way for President Donald Trump's executive order limiting the method to be used in November's elections.

The provisions are still subject to additional legal challenges and may not go into effect in time to meet the tight deadline to change procedures for the midterm elections. They would forbid the Postal Service from sending mail ballots from any state that does not comply with Trump's order and would require an overhaul of the envelopes containing the ballots.

Despite the high court's initial clearance of the order, it did not decide on the constitutionality of the new regulation— only on whether the challenge was premature when Democratic-controlled states persuaded a federal judge in Boston to suspend them in June. A second ruling from the same judge would prevent the Postal Service from implementing any procedural changes before this year's midterms and would likely need to be nullified, as well.

Time is running out for the administration to make any changes in the nation's voting procedures. The first mail ballots are required to be sent to military and overseas voters from North Carolina on Sept. 4. At that point, it would be virtually impossible for all states to alter the formatting of their mail ballots to comply with Trump's directive. The Postal Service rule also requires states to submit voter lists in order to get their mail ballots delivered.

The Postal Service said it could not comment on its rule given the litigation.

Lawyers from Democratic-run states and civil rights groups who sued to block the order argued that Trump doesn't have the authority to change election regulations in states. The U.S. Constitution vests that power in the states or Congress, which has been unable to pass Trump's desired election changes.

The Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court last month to let it move forward with the executive order, which calls for the federal government to compile a list of eligible voters and send mail ballots only to those on the list.

title: Police find the body of Karen Solomon, who was sought in the killing of her police officer husband
description: A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead Monday, six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said.  Karen Solomon, an advocat...
fullText:
A mental health advocate suspected of killing her police officer husband was found dead Monday, six days after she disappeared from her Massachusetts home, authorities said.

Karen Solomon, an advocate who called for improvements and greater awareness of police mental health issues, had disappeared after Worcester Police Officer Kurt Solomon was found dead at their home just before 5:30 a.m. on Aug. 18. Officials had named Karen Solomon a suspect and said she was believed to be armed.

"We believe this case is a tragic murder-suicide that occurred," Worcester Police Chief Paul Saucier said at a news conference Monday.

Two people who worked at Fairlawn Rehabilitation Hospital reported finding human remains nearby, and officers recovered a woman's corpse, Saucier said. A final ID was still pending, but authorities said they were confident it was Karen Solomon.

A handgun found near her body was not a Worcester police service weapon, and investigators were working to determine who owned it.

On Aug. 19, authorities released doorbell camera footage of Karen Solomon walking down a street in a T-shirt, shorts and flip-flops, just minutes after officers responded to the couple's home and found her husband's body.

Kurt Solomon, who had served 31 years with the police department, was mortally injured with a sharp object, authorities have said.

Worcester County District Attorney Joseph Early Jr. said Karen Solomon had been at the house on the morning of her husband's death, and investigators were looking to question her. An arrest warrant issued over the weekend charged her with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

Police handed out flyers with her photo to drivers in the area. An intensive law enforcement search that included local, state and federal agencies centered on the area near the couple's Worcester home and a reservoir about a mile (1.6 kilometers) away. Authorities had deployed drones, boats and tracking dogs.

Karen Solomon, 58, co-founded the group First H.E.L.P., which advocates for the mental health of police officers. She also wrote two books — "Hearts Beneath the Badge" and "The Price They Pay" — about the physical and psychological experiences of first responders.

In a 2020 interview on the "Dr. Phil" show with Phil McGraw, she said police departments often offered little help to the families of officers who took their own lives.

In a statement read by Saucier during Monday's news conference, the Solomon family thanked law enforcement for helping them find some answers.

"The nightmare of the past week has left our family heartbroken and rudderless," the family said. "The compassion, dedication and empathy of all agencies involved have given us light in face of darkness."

A wake for Kurt Solomon was scheduled for Tuesday, and his funeral for Wednesday, the police chief said. The local police union president, Thomas Duffy, described him as "a tremendous human being" who was like family.

Nvidia worker, 8 others smuggled AI servers into China, Taiwan says
description: Employees of Nvidia and Sun Micro were part of a scheme to smuggle AI servers into China, according to prosecutors in Taiwan.
fullText:
TAIPEI (Reuters) - Taiwan prosecutors said on Monday they had indicted nine people, including employees of Nvidia and Super Micro, over involvement in the illegal export of artificial intelligence servers to China.

Semiconductor powerhouse Taiwan is the world's largest producer of advanced chips used in AI applications. Prosecutors this year investigated the suspected illegal export of servers equipped with Nvidia chips subject to U.S. export controls.

Washington has imposed curbs since 2022 making it illegal for such semiconductors to be exported or sold in China without a license.

Eight people, including one employee of Nvidia's Taiwan unit and two employees of Super Micro's Taiwan unit, were charged with breach of trust and document forgery in connection with the illegal export of high-end AI servers, prosecutors in the port city of Keelung said in a statement.

Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.

A ninth defendant was charged in a related case involving the alleged siphoning of funds from a distributor company involved, the statement said, without providing the full names of any of the defendants.

The alleged scheme involved making it appear that 130 B300 servers ordered from Super Micro would be installed and used at a rented server facility in Taiwan.

Prosecutors said false end-user documents stated that the servers would be installed in Taiwan.

Of those 130 servers, 74 were ultimately exported and delivered to Chinese customers through routes that included direct shipments to China as well as transhipments through Indonesia, Japan and Hong Kong, they said.

The remaining 56 servers were intended to be exported to a company in Japan, prosecutors said, but Taiwan customs officials detected irregularities and stopped their export.

The prosecutors said the defendants were "fully aware" that both Nvidia and Super Micro have "rigorous internal control procedures" regarding exports.

However, the defendants "colluded with one another at various levels for enormous profit, illegally exporting high-end servers, increasing corporate compliance costs, and severely damaging our nation's international image", they added.

Taiwan has tightened export controls in recent years to keep advanced technology and know-how from reaching China, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory despite the strong objections of the island's government.

description: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has promised to deport thousands of migrants who are in the country without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as he attempts to make significant chang...
fullText:
BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has promised to deport thousands of migrants who are in the country without residence permits, mainly Venezuelans, as he attempts to make significant changes to the nation's immigration policies that he says will reduce crime.

De la Espriella, who was sworn into office three weeks ago, said that he would order the country's national immigration service to conduct raids with Colombian police as early as this week. He announced the new policy in a video released on Sunday night in his X account where he spoke of multiple measures to reduce crime and confront criminal groups.

The ultra conservative leader, who is closely aligned with the U.S. President Donald Trump, said that law enforcement will first target migrants who are "committing crimes" and then, those who are living in the country without regular status.

"I will not accept any illegal immigrants, wherever they come from," de la Espriella said in the video. "They will have to leave and be deported. It is a political decision I am taking responsibility for."

Most migrants living in Colombia come from neighboring Venezuela, a nation that lost about a fifth of its population over the past decade as Venezuelans fled a repressive regime that oversaw years of economic turmoil, and a 75% contraction in the nation's GDP.

Around 2.8 million Venezuelans were living in Colombia as of August, according to the United Nations, making it the largest Venezuelan diaspora. In July, Colombia's national immigration service said that it had granted temporary residence permits to about 2.3 million Venezuelans under a scheme rolled out in 2021 by then President Ivan Duque during the peak of Venezuela's immigration crisis.

De la Espriella's effort to deport migrants who have no regular status marks a major shift for Colombia, which had long worked to protect incoming Venezuelans and grant them a pathway towards permanent residency.

Ana Karina García, director of Juntos Se Puede, an organization that helps Venezuelan migrants in Colombia, said that the Colombian government stopped handing out new temporary residency permits three years ago. She said that de la Espriella's incoming administration should expand pathways to legal residency, instead of punishing people who cannot obtain residency permits.

"We understand that the president wants to protect Colombians," she said. "But there is no need to protect them from migrants. It has been proven that foreigners do not commit crimes at greater rates" than the local population.

Arles Pereda, the president of an association that represents Venezuelans in Bogota, said the announcement worried him, because new groups of Venezuelans displaced by the twin earthquakes that rocked the country in June have been arriving in Colombia to seek opportunities.

"The doors seem to be closing," Pereda said. "Not just in Colombia, but also in Chile, Peru and Ecuador," where conservative leaders have also made it harder for Venezuelan migrants to get residency permits.

In a text message, Colombia's national immigration department, Migracion Colombia, said that the agency is currently without a director. The agency said it will only implement the new policies outlined by Colombia's incoming government once a new director is appointed and installed. ___
